lines.text: At midnight, my house turned one hundred years old. This morning, my front door is *gone.* Just wall.
In Japan there's an old legend. When an object survives a hundred years, it gets a *soul.* They call it tsukumogami.
Old umbrellas hop around on one leg. Paper lanterns open their mouths. Sandals walk off on their own.
People used to throw things out right before they turned a hundred. Just in case. Because the ones that woke up *angry* got even.
My great-grandfather built this house in 1926. Last night, as a joke, I put one candle on a cupcake. Happy birthday, house.
There's a sign in the yard. *For sale.* I move out on Friday.
At midnight, every light in the house dimmed at once. Like it was *taking a breath.*
Then the floors creaked. Every room, all at the same time. Like something waking up and *stretching.*
The front door locked itself. Then every window. Click. Click. Click.
Upstairs, the hallway was longer. Doors I'd never seen. Rooms with *no windows.*
I ran for the front door. I grabbed the handle. It was *warm.*
Behind me, the candle blew out. And the walls spoke, in a voice like old wood bending.
This morning, there's no front door. Just smooth wall. And the For Sale sign is lying in the yard. *Snapped in half.*
